Paper Content:
Discontinuous Galerkin discretization of conservative
dynamical low-rank approximation schemes for the
Vlasov–Poisson equation
Andr´e Uschmajew∗
Andreas Zeiser†
Abstract
A numerical dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) scheme for the solution of the
Vlasov–Poisson equation is presented. Based on the formulation of the DLRA equations as
Friedrichs’ systems in a continuous setting, it combines recently proposed conservative DLRA
methods with a discontinuous Galerkin discretization. The resulting scheme is shown to ensure
mass and momentum conservation at the discrete level. In addition, a new formulation of the
conservative integrator is proposed which facilitates a projector splitting integrator. Numerical
experiments validate our approach in oneand two-dimensional simulations of Landau damping.
As a demonstration of feasibility, it is also shown that the rank-adaptive unconventional
integrator can be combined with mesh adaptivity.
1

For d = 2, 3 the numerical solution of the Vlasov–Poisson equation is challenging, since a

Recently, dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) [18] has been proposed in the seminal

and its time evolution is applied to the spatial and velocity components separately. The general
idea of low-rank approximation has been demonstrated to be highly effective for the Vlasov–Poisson
equation in several works [1, 13, 14, 15]. A comprehensive literature survey can be found in [8].
As for DLRA methods, a recent research focus has been on the development of conservative
methods, which is somewhat non-trivial to achieve. The ideas developed in [7] allowed for significant
progress in this direction. By combining them with the rank-adaptive unconventional integrator
from [4], also called basis update and Galerkin (BUG) integrator [3], the recent work [10] presents a
robust numerical time stepping scheme for the factors Xi, Sij and Vj in the DLRA representation (3)
which is mass and momentum conservative and allows the rank r to be chosen adaptively.
The goal of the present work is to combine the conservative DLRA integrator from [10] with
a discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretization. This is motivated by the fact that the governing
equations for the DLRA factors in the continuous setting take the form of Friedrichs’ systems, as
worked out in [21]. DG methods possess favorable numerical properties for solving such systems, and,
in addition, offer the possibility for adaptive mesh refinement. We make two main contributions.
First, for a fixed discretization, we obtain a rank-adaptive and conservative DG-based DLRA
approximation scheme for the Vlasov–Poisson equation. Second, we demonstrate how our approach
of first formulating the DLRA scheme in a continuous setting and then discretizing the subproblems
allows us to exploit the capabilities of DG solvers regarding mesh adaptivity. Compared to, e.g., [15],
where the DLRA approach is applied to a full DG discretization of a linear kinetic equation, this
approach offers much more flexibility. While the mesh adaptive version of our solver in its current
form does not yet yield a conservative scheme due to the coarsening steps, we believe this approach
to be a promising route for further development.
In more detail, the outline and contributions of the paper can be summarized as follows. In
section 2 we derive the equations of motion for the DLRA approach. We review the standard DLRA
integrators in section 2.1 and the required modifications for the conservative integrator as proposed
in [7, 10] in section 2.2. We pay special attention to formulating the equations in a continuous
setting as Friedrichs’ systems in weak form, which makes it easier to enable spatially adaptive DG
discretizations later. Our derivation of the equations for the conservative integrator in section 2.3
is based on a slightly different tangent space decomposition compared to [7, 10]. In particular,
we present a new version of the modified L-step using a suitable block QR decomposition of the
DLRA representation, which avoids forming normal equations. This L-step is then included in
the rank-adaptive unconventional integrator, which is introduced in section 2.4. As a secondary
result, our special QR representation also suggests a projector-splitting integrator allowing for fixed
velocity basis functions which has not been featured in the original works. However, as we show
in the numerical experiments, the projector splitting version is not conservative, and hence the
unconventional integrator must to be used.
Section 3 presents the main theoretical contribution. We introduce the DG discretization for
the DLRA equations in sections 3.1 and 3.2. Special attention is paid to the approximation of
derivatives and numerical fluxes at the element interfaces. As explained in [7, 10], the conservation
properties of time integrators can be ensured by enforcing discrete counterparts of certain continuity
equations arising in the Vlasov–Poisson system. In section 3.3, we rigorously prove these discrete
continuity equations for mass and momentum conservation under the assumption that central fluxes
are used in the DG discretization and the explicit Euler method is applied for time-stepping. The
proof holds for arbitrary spatial dimensions. In section 3.4, we discuss spatial adaptivity in the DG
discretization, though currently in a simplified form.
Finally, in section 4 we present numerical simulations that illustrate the feasibility and advantages
of our approach, and confirm the theoretical findings. As a main contribution, we present simulations
for Landau damping in two spatial dimensions with conservation of mass and momentum in
section 4.2. We also demonstrate the use of spatial adaptivity for a 2d transport problem in 4.3.
While these experiments are still conducted in a simplified setting of periodic boundaries, they
serve as an important proof of concept that DG methods can be successfully used for the DLRA
simulation of Vlasov–Poisson equations.

2.2
Conservative DLRA integrators
In order to achieve conservation of mass and momentum, the standard DLRA integrator must
be modified. The key idea is to replace the non-conservative discretization of the S-step with a
conservative one. As mentioned in the introduction, this approach was first presented in [7] and
further developed in [10]. The S-step is the only step where the basis functions Xi(t) and Vj(t)
are fixed, so the ODE (11) is the only part of the DLRA scheme that changes with time. Hence,
if we can modify this ODE to be conservative, the overall DLRA scheme becomes conservative.
To this end, [7] proposed a modified L-step in the context of a different basis update strategy,
while [10] presented a new version of the L-step using a QR decomposition, which avoids forming
normal equations. The latter approach is used here for the conservative DLRA integrator, as it is
more suitable for the DG discretization of the Vlasov–Poisson equation.
3
As a result, the modified L-step is given by the following procedure: given an initial S(0) = S0,
we compute the time derivative ∂tS(t) = S’(t) such that
∂tS(t) + B(v)·∂vS(t) − E(t,x)B(x)·∂xS(t) = 0,
(12)
where B(v) and B(x) are suitable matrices. But since this equation is not conservative, we need
to modify it to enforce conservation. To do this, we use the following approach:

First, we decompose the space of S(t) into a sum of two subspaces: one that is orthogonal to the
numerical fluxes and one that is not. This decomposition allows us to split the equation into two parts,
one of which can be modified to ensure conservation while leaving the other part unchanged.

Then, we form a modified equation for the non-orthogonal part by adding a suitable term that ensures
conservation. This term is constructed using a block QR decomposition of the DLRA representation,
which avoids forming normal equations and thus preserves the structure of the problem.

Finally, we combine the modified equation with the original equation for the orthogonal part to obtain
a new system that is conservative.

This approach is detailed in [10], and the resulting modified L-step is given by the following equation:

∂tS(t) + B(v)·∂vS(t) − E(t,x)B(x)·∂xS(t) + (Q(t)·S(t))·R(t) = 0,

(13)

where Q(t) and R(t) are matrices obtained from the block QR decomposition of S(t). This ensures
that the modified equation is conservative, while still maintaining the structure of the original equation.

Once the modified L-step is implemented, the overall DLRA scheme becomes conservative, as the
S-step is the only part that changes with time, and the modified L-step ensures that the mass and
momentum are conserved at each time step.

In addition to the modified L-step, the conservative DLRA integrator also includes a modified S-step
that uses a different basis update strategy, which avoids the need to form normal equations and thus
preserves the structure of the problem. This is important for the DG discretization, as it allows for
the use of central fluxes, which are necessary for the conservation properties of the scheme.

Finally, the conservative DLRA integrator is completed by the modified K-step and L-step, which are
now designed to be compatible with the modified S-step and ensure that the overall scheme is mass
and momentum conservative.

In summary, the conservative DLRA integrator is built by combining the standard K-step and L-step
with the modified S-step, which is designed to ensure conservation. This results in a scheme that is
both structure-preserving and conservative, making it suitable for the DG discretization of the Vlasov–
Poisson equation.
